finding: S1 constrains only the state the suite LEAVES ('running the suite leaves spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ byte-identical'), but properties 7 and 8 need the panel to be constant ACROSS the N+1 invocations they compare, and §2.2 records that every emitting invocation rewrites the round snapshot. §4.1 then makes the panel a function of that snapshot: regression is appended when the spec has changed since the snapshot OR findings were resolved fixed, and §4.1's own round-3 row is the measured case where neither half held. So the first, unrestricted invocation can refresh the snapshot, make the spec-changed half false for every per-role invocation that follows, and — on any spec where no finding carries a fixed disposition — drop regression from the per-role emissions. The concatenation then differs from the unrestricted payload for a reason that has nothing to do with --role, and the release gate passes or fails according to the order the test happens to invoke in. Nothing in §6 fixes that order or that constancy.
suggestion: Add a condition to §6.1 stating the property the comparison actually needs — every invocation in one property-7 comparison observes the same review state, so the panel it would emit is identical — rather than only the after-the-fact equality S1 states. Keep it a property (constant panel across the comparison), not a harness recipe.

finding: Properties 3 and 9 both compare the emission against a pre-clause emission — 'both sides taken from the same tree' (3) and 'the same tree's pre-clause emission' (9) — and §6.3 withdraws both mechanisms that could produce that side: the cross-version baseline (withdrawn because 'a go test binary compiles one tree; the old emitter is not callable from the new one') and the production toggle to emit without the clauses. No third mechanism is named anywhere in §6. So the two properties have no producible left-hand side. The one construction still available — strip the known 468-byte suffix off the emitted prompt and compare the remainder — turns both properties into tautologies that cannot fail for any implementation already satisfying property 1, which is the failure mode CLAUDE.md's run-do-not-read rule exists to catch.
suggestion: Either name the baseline as an implementation seam a task owns (a builder that assembles the body without the append, callable from the test), or restate 3 and 9 as properties of the emitted artifact alone: property 1 already fixes the suffix, so 3 collapses to 'the appended suffix is 468 bytes and the byte preceding it is not LF' and 9 becomes redundant and can be deleted. A property that cannot fail costs a round every time a reviewer re-derives that it cannot.

finding: Properties 3 and 9 both require a pre-clause emission from the same tree, and §6.3 — twelve lines later — records that both mechanisms capable of producing one were withdrawn. Property 3: "The net length change per affected prompt is exactly 467 bytes, both sides taken from the same tree." Property 9: "the payload differs from the same tree's pre-clause emission only by §2.3's construction." §6.3 withdraws "A cross-version baseline (v0.35.2's emitter)" because "a go test binary compiles one tree", and "A production toggle to emit 'without the clauses'" because it "buys a seam whose only false caller is a test". Property 3's own qualifier "both sides taken from the same tree" is precisely the sentence that forecloses the first, and the toggle was the only same-tree route to the second side. The one residue — reconstructing the baseline by stripping the known suffix from the emitted prompt — makes both properties tautologies (asserting 468 == 468 against a constant this spec supplies), which is the class §6.3 says it exists to retire. §6's preamble deferring the harness to "a task's acceptance" does not rescue this: the deferral is to an empty set, because §6.3 has already ruled on every candidate.
suggestion: Either restate properties 3 and 9 as properties of the emitted artifact that need no baseline (e.g. "an affected prompt ends with §2.3's construction and its body's last byte before that construction is not LF", which is falsifiable against one emission), or reinstate one mechanism in §6.3 with the cost accepted. As written the section demands a measurement it also forbids.

finding: Properties 4 and 12 cannot both be implemented. Property 4 requires `--role <name>` to leave "every other top-level key unchanged"; property 12 requires that "Under `--role`, `review_loop.instruction` is a sentence-subset of the unrestricted one and contains none of that key's orchestrator-addressed directives". Measured on the shipped binary (`tp review spec/0.36.0.md`), the payload's top-level keys are exactly `spec, spec_ref, spec_path, structured_elements, skipped_roles, prompts, review_loop` — so `review_loop` IS one of the "other top-level keys" property 4 freezes, and §4.2.3 establishes that the unrestricted instruction does carry orchestrator-addressed directives ("For each prompt, spawn a sub-agent via the Agent tool… Process the regression prompt first"), so a conformant `--role` payload MUST change it. Whichever an implementer builds, one of the two properties fails, and property 4 is the one §6.2 lists first — so the natural reading (freeze everything but `prompts[]`) silently reinstates exactly the broken contract §4.2.3 was written to fix. This is the same clause round 5 flagged as missing at §4.2 (`payload-keys-under-role-unspecified`); the repair added it back without excepting the key the release changes.
suggestion: Scope property 4 to the keys the release does not touch: "…with every top-level key other than `prompts` and `review_loop` unchanged", and add a sentence naming `review_loop` as the one exception with property 12 as its rule. If `skipped_roles` is also reduced under `--role` (§4.2.1 says only that the named role's entry is "present"), say so in the same property rather than leaving "unchanged" to decide it by default.

finding: Properties 4 and 12 cannot both be satisfied, so no engineer can write both tests. Property 4 requires --role to leave 'every other top-level key unchanged'. review_loop IS a top-level key of the emitted payload — measured on this spec's own round-10 emission the top-level keys are spec, spec_ref, spec_path, structured_elements, skipped_roles, prompts, review_loop — and property 12 requires review_loop.instruction to be a strict sentence-subset under --role. One engineer asserts the payload minus prompts[] is byte-identical; another asserts review_loop.instruction shrank. Exactly one of the two tests can pass, and §6.2 gives no way to tell which was intended.
suggestion: Narrow property 4 to 'every other top-level key except review_loop unchanged, and review_loop unchanged apart from the instruction edit property 12 fixes', and repeat the carve-out in §4.2 where the reduction is first described.

finding: Property 4 and property 12 cannot both hold. Property 4: "--role <name> emits exactly one prompts[] entry, byte-identical to that role's entry in the otherwise identical invocation without the flag, with every other top-level key unchanged." Property 12: "Under --role, review_loop.instruction is a sentence-subset of the unrestricted one and contains none of that key's orchestrator-addressed directives." Measured on this spec's own round-10 emission, the payload's top-level keys are spec, spec_ref, spec_path, structured_elements, skipped_roles, prompts, review_loop — so review_loop IS a top-level key, and property 12 requires it to change under exactly the flag property 4 says leaves every other top-level key unchanged. An implementer satisfying property 4 fails property 12 and vice versa, and §6 is the release's acceptance surface, so there is no lower altitude at which this resolves.
suggestion: Scope property 4's invariance clause to the keys the flag is not specified to touch: "with every other top-level key unchanged except review_loop.instruction, which property 12 governs." §4.2.3 already argues that the instruction edit is deliberate; property 4 is the only place that contradicts it.

finding: Property 5 asks for the exit-0 branch "for each of the five reasons §4.2.1 tabulates", and no single command can produce all five — the table is a union across `tp review` and `tp audit` presented as one taxonomy, and property 5, unlike property 6, never scopes itself to "each command's own flag set". Measured by locating every construction site of `engine.SkippedRole` in the tree: `no-checklist-items` is set in exactly one place, `internal/cli/audit_roles.go:335`, on the AUDIT path (`len(items) == 0` over the role's git-diff-derived file check items) and nowhere in the review emitter; `no-spec-change` is set in exactly one place, `internal/cli/review.go:856`, guarded by `if diffFrom != ""` — and `tp audit` registers no `--diff-from` (§4.2.2 verifies this), so audit can never produce it; `no-baseline` is set at `internal/cli/review.go:908` under `round < 2` for `engine.RegressionRoleID` only, and §4.1 establishes there is no regression role in the audit phase. So `tp review --role X` cannot exhibit `no-checklist-items`, and `tp audit --role X` cannot exhibit `no-spec-change` or `no-baseline`. An implementer told to build one fixture per reason has no command to run three of them under, and property 5's five-way iteration cannot be written as stated.
suggestion: Split property 5 by command, the way property 6 already is: `tp review` owns `domain-mismatch`, `disabled-by-spec`, `no-spec-change` and `no-baseline`; `tp audit` owns `domain-mismatch`, `disabled-by-spec` and `no-checklist-items`. Then either annotate §4.2.1's table with a Command column, or state under it that the five rows are the union across both commands and no invocation sees all five.

finding: §4.2.1 justifies the whole exit-0 rule with two bolded table rows — "The two rows in bold are the failure: a corpus role with an empty checklist is spawned as a unit and emits no prompt, so under an exit-2 rule its own brief would fail before it did any work" — and neither row can occur on the review path the brief of §4.2.3 creates. Round 8 already established that the second row (`no-spec-change`) cannot, because the brief carries no `--diff-from`. The first row is measured here and is worse than underspecified: `no-checklist-items` is emitted from exactly one site in the tree, `internal/cli/audit_roles.go:335`, and its predicate is `len(items) == 0` where `items` comes from `fileCheckItems(files, role.ID)` over the git-diff-selected code files — an AUDIT-phase quantity. `internal/cli/review.go` never constructs it. So for a `review-role` unit — half the units §4.2.3's brief change covers, and the half §4.1's whole measurement is about — §4.2.1 states no reachable instance of the failure it exists to prevent, while the two skips review CAN produce (`domain-mismatch`, `disabled-by-spec`) both drop the unit too and so never strand a brief. An implementer reading §4.2.1 cannot tell whether the exit-0 rule is required on the review path at all, or is audit-only behaviour stated once for both.
suggestion: State the phase each bolded row belongs to. Concretely: for `tp audit`, `no-checklist-items` is the live case and the exit-0 rule is load-bearing; for `tp review`, name the reachable case that strands a brief or say plainly that none exists today and the rule is defensive there. Adding a Command column to the skip table makes both statements fall out of the table instead of the prose.

finding: §4.2.3 answers the `review_loop.instruction` problem with a filter — 'no sentence may direct an action the caller's own payload cannot support' — and §6.2 property 12 concedes the predicate is 'a reading, not a computation' needing a task-owned fixture. Measured on this round's own payload (round 10, this spec, current binary): the key is 733 bytes in six sentences, and five of them direct the orchestrator (spawn a sub-agent per prompt; merge/verify/record; repeat until --status --check exits 0; process the regression prompt first; run the uncounted --perspective regression delta pass). Exactly one sentence survives the filter — 'Read the spec at <path> before processing each prompt.', 109 bytes — and its content is already in the payload twice: the top-level `spec_path` key, and the prompt body's own line 'Read the spec file before reviewing. The spec is NOT included inline to save context.' (verified in this unit's prompt). Under `--spec-inline` the surviving sentence is moot instead of duplicated. So the release buys a filter over nine assignment sites plus an admittedly undecidable fixture in order to emit 109 bytes that duplicate two existing surfaces, and saves 624 of 733 where 733 was available.
suggestion: Under `--role`, omit `review_loop.instruction` entirely and say so. The honest subset carries no information the payload does not already hold; absence is mechanically decidable, so property 12 collapses to 'under --role the key is absent; without --role it is unchanged' — no sentence taxonomy, no fixture, no reading; and no existing caller is affected because `--role` ships in this release. §6.3's fourth row records that the enumerated list was measured short by one and its semantic replacement was undecidable — absence is the third option neither draft tried. If the key must remain present for shape reasons, emit it as the empty string on the same reasoning.

finding: §4.4 and Non-Goal 6 cite each other and one of the two citations is false. §4.4: "Non-Goal 6 records where it should land and that nothing there covers it yet." Non-Goal 6 says the opposite of its first clause: "No spec contains that section today, and §3.1's rule applies here too: this one names no owner either." There is no "where it should land" for §4.4 to be pointing at — Non-Goal 6 deliberately declines to name one, on the rule §3.1 states in terms ("Naming a file that does not contain the question is worse than naming none"). So §4.4 reads as a promise of a routing decision that the section it cites was written specifically to withhold, and a reader following the pointer finds the refusal rather than the destination. This is the failure mode §3.1 legislated against, executed one section later in a weaker form: not a wrong filename, but a claim that a filename exists.
suggestion: Change §4.4's sentence to match its target: "Non-Goal 6 records that no spec owns this yet." That keeps the pointer honest and preserves §3.1's rule, which is the only thing making the omission deliberate rather than an oversight.

finding: §6.3 withdraws the only named mechanism for S1 on a new factual premise — "A `TestMain` bracket for S1 | `TestMain` is per-package and these tests span packages" — and that premise creates a hazard S1 does not address and no per-package repair can reach. `go test ./...` builds one binary per package and runs them CONCURRENTLY (default `-p` is GOMAXPROCS). Every emission writes `snapshot-round-N.md` through `engine.WriteSnapshotAtomic` (`internal/cli/review.go:1865`, `internal/cli/audit.go:475`) into a directory `engine.ReviewStateDir` derives from the spec's own path with no override — the very fact §6.1 cites. So two packages whose tests emit against the same spec write the same directory at the same time, and `WriteSnapshotAtomic`'s tmp+rename is atomic per write but does not serialise two writers or restore a prior value. S1 asks for a byte-identical outcome over `spec/.tp-review/` and `.tp/rounds/`; after §6.3's withdrawal the spec names no mechanism at all, and an implementer cannot supply one at package scope because the state is shared across the packages, not within them. Property 8 makes this concrete rather than hypothetical: the gate iterates the repository's own specs, so the racing writers are the repository's real review state.
suggestion: Make S1 a suite-level statement with a suite-level mechanism, since §6.3 has established the scope is the suite: either require the emitting tests to run serialised (`-p 1` for the affected packages, or a single package that owns every emission) and say so, or require every emitting test to operate on a copied spec tree and state that S1 is then trivially satisfied because nothing under the repository root is written at all. Naming which of the two is chosen is what makes the condition buildable; §6.3 having removed the third option, leaving the choice open leaves S1 with no implementation.

finding: Property 10 requires that the brief command, 'running it, exits 0', but nothing pins how a test runs it, and the two available readings have different fault coverage. brief_command is a string (tp review <spec> --role <id>); executing it as a command line needs a tp on PATH, which under go test is an installed release rather than the tree under test — §6.3 already records that a go test binary compiles one tree. The alternative, parsing the string and invoking the command function in-process, proves the flag is accepted but cannot catch a brief_command that is well-formed as a string and malformed as a command line (an unquoted spec path, a stale flag name, a missing separator) — which is precisely the class §4.2.3 exists to prevent, since the release's only change outside the emitter is the string itself. Two engineers write tests that agree on the property and disagree on what it rules out.
suggestion: Say which reading the property requires — most plausibly 'the emitted string, executed as a command line against a binary built from this tree' — or split property 10 in two: the string equals the form §4.2.3 fixes, and the flag it names is accepted by that command's own flag set.

finding: Property 2 ('No prompt whose output_path is empty contains either clause') can pass while matching zero prompts, because nothing in the spec requires any prompt to HAVE an empty output_path. §2.2 states only that output_path is 'a key both commands emit'. Property 2's own qualifier — that the modes producing such a prompt are every --perspective value plus --verify — is written as a derivation of the test's INPUT set, not as a requirement on the emitter, so it is an assumption the property rests on rather than an assertion the property makes. If a --perspective or --verify prompt carries a non-empty output_path, the test filters to the empty set, reports green, and §2.3's emission predicate has no negative case at all — the clause reaches prompts §2.3 says it must not, and the only property guarding that is the one that just passed.
suggestion: Split it: state the emitter-side fact as its own property ('a prompt emitted under any --perspective value, or under --verify, carries an empty output_path'), then have property 2 assert the absence of the clauses over that set. A property whose input set can legitimately be empty needs a companion that fixes the set as non-empty.

finding: Property 5 is the largest build task in §6 and the spec names none of the preconditions its fixtures need, each of which is a non-obvious property of the shipped code rather than of the spec. Measured: (a) `domain-mismatch` is produced only by `engine.DomainSkippedRoles`, which returns `[]SkippedRole{}` whenever `LoadRoleCorpus` reports the corpus unpopulated — its own comment says "the embedded corpus is domain-selected, never domain-filtered, so no role is skipped for a domain mismatch" — so the fixture needs a populated USER corpus under `.tp/reviewers/`+`.tp/auditors/` at the fixture root AND a `domain:` in the spec frontmatter AND a role whose `domains` omits it; (b) `disabled-by-spec` comes from `ResolveOverrideFocus`'s drop set, which by its own doc comment holds only roles still active after domain filtering, so its fixture must not double as (a)'s; (c) `no-spec-change` fires only when `engine.RoleFocusOutsideDiff` returns true, which requires at least one `focus` entry carrying a literal `§N.M` cross-reference ("generic questions with no § reference keep the role emitted") plus a non-empty diff plus `--diff-from` plus `--round >= 2`; (d) `no-checklist-items` needs an audit invocation whose `git diff` selection yields zero items for that one role, i.e. a working tree with history. §7 measured that this repository supplies none of these ("zero specs carry `enabled: false` and zero carry a `domain`"), and §6.1's only permitted isolation — relocating the spec — resolves the corpus from the relocated root and so hands back the embedded default, which makes (a) and (c) unreachable by construction.
suggestion: Under property 5, state that each of the four fixture-built reasons requires a purpose-built role corpus co-located with the fixture spec, and name the shape each needs (a `domains` mismatch, an `enabled: false` frontmatter override, a `§`-scoped `focus`, an audit tree whose diff selects no files for the role). Say explicitly that the fixture corpus is deliberately not this repository's, so it does not read as a violation of §6.1.

finding: §6.3's fourth row withdraws "An enumerated list of forbidden directives for property 12" for two independent reasons — "Measured short by one; its semantic replacement was undecidable" — and property 12 then requires both of the things just withdrawn. Its normative half is the semantic predicate ("contains none of that key's orchestrator-addressed directives"), which §6.3 calls undecidable; its operational half is "Which sentences are orchestrator-addressed is a fixture the task owns", which is the enumerated list §6.3 calls measured short. Moving the enumeration from the spec to a task's acceptance changes its address, not its defect: the same list, written by the same reading, is still short by one and now has no recorded derivation to check it against. §4.2.3 makes the same commitment in the opposite direction — "The rule is a property, not a list of sentences to delete" — so three sections now give three different answers to how property 12 is discharged.
suggestion: Pick one and let the other two cite it. The decidable option is a structural predicate over the assembled string rather than a reading: e.g. "under --role, instruction contains no sentence whose imperative names an artifact absent from this payload" — mechanical against the nine assignment sites §4.2.3 identifies. If no decidable form exists, say so in §6.3 and drop property 12 to a task note rather than a release property.

finding: The release gate's subject set is not enumerable from the text, and the gate's evidence was measured on a different set than the gate runs on. §6.2 property 8 says 'every spec in the repository an unrestricted invocation emits prompts for'; §7's breadth argument is measured over '22 version specs, 5 KB to 79 KB, 15 with recorded rounds and 7 with none'. Measured on this tree: spec/ holds 39 .md files; 6 are companion documents (-candidates, -guard-tests, -release-counts, -role-prompt-research); 33 carry a version number; and exactly 22 have a bare <version>.md filename — so §7's 22 is the bare-filename set, which reconciles only if you already know that rule. The 11 older specs (0.11.0-review.md through 0.22.0-section-normalization.md) are version specs by CLAUDE.md's own Project Structure listing and are excluded by a filter §7 never states. An engineer implementing property 8 from its own words runs the gate over 39 candidates, not 22.
suggestion: State the set as a predicate a test evaluates — for example every spec/*.md for which an unrestricted invocation exits 0 and emits at least one prompt — and let the count be whatever that predicate yields, or keep the 22 and name the filter (filename matches <version>.md exactly) in the same sentence. §7's breadth claim is only as good as a set the gate can reproduce.

finding: §1.1's closing paragraph justifies unconditional emission with an impossibility claim the mechanism sections refute: "The clauses are emitted on every path… tp emits the prompt before anything knows which runner will consume it, so a conditional emission is not computable at the point of emission." §2.3 then specifies exactly a conditional emission computed at the point of emission — "The clauses are appended to every prompt whose output_path is non-empty, and to no other" — and §6.2 property 2 fixes the excluded set as every --perspective value plus --verify. So the release does condition emission; what is not computable is conditioning on the runner specifically, and §1.1 never says so. As written the two sections disagree on whether a condition exists, and §1.1's arithmetic compounds it by pricing the change "per role prompt" when §2.3's predicate is over prompts with a non-empty output_path — sets §4.2 itself shows are different, since --perspective testing emits a prompt carrying role test-planner.
suggestion: Qualify the claim to the variable it is actually about: "a condition on which runner will consume the prompt is not computable at the point of emission; the condition tp does apply is §2.3's, on output_path." Then price the delta over the set property 2 selects rather than over "role prompt".

finding: §2.3's Emission predicate paragraph ends: "That is the positive statement §6.2 property 2 states the negative of; §4.4 records why the predicate is a property of the prompt rather than of the role." §4.4 records nothing of the kind. Its two paragraphs are entirely about the regression prompt reaching four units and no unit, the driver defect in BuildNextUnits, Non-Goal 6, and §6.2 property 11 — the words output_path, predicate and prompt-versus-role do not occur in it. So the single justification for choosing a prompt-level predicate over a role-level one has no home in the document. That matters beyond a broken pointer: the prompt/role distinction is what §4.2.1's whole exit-0 rule turns on (the unit set and the emitted set are computed by different filters), so the choice is load-bearing and is now unargued. Both sections were edited this round, which is how the two halves came apart.
suggestion: Either move the one-sentence rationale into §4.4 (the regression prompt is the worked example: it is a prompt with a writer named and no role assigned), or state it inline in §2.3 and drop the cross-reference. A justification that lives in neither section is the same defect §1.1 records the figure index dying of.

finding: §3.2's clause is emitted byte-identically to every unit on every path and its second sentence is false on one of them. The clause: "A run that dies with its rows unwritten loses the whole round; a partially written file is still usable." §3.1 establishes the opposite under tp run: the unit writes role-<id>.ndjson.part, "the driver renames it to the final name only on exit 0", so "a unit that dies therefore leaves rows that are never promoted, and a truncated trailing line would fail the predicate even if they were" — the file is recoverable by a human later, which is not what "usable" says to an agent deciding how to spend its round. §2.3 forbids fixing this by conditioning the text, and §1.1 prices unconditional emission as deliberate, so the driver-spawned unit is told a salvage story §3.1 spent a subsection refusing to extend to it. §3.1 is careful about this in its own voice ("interactive-path results, and they do not carry to tp run unchanged"); the clause it governs is not.
suggestion: Make the clause's second sentence true on both paths by claiming only what §3.1 grants: "…loses the whole round; a partially written file preserves every row already written." That is the fact both paths share, it still motivates the behaviour, and it costs bytes §1.1 can re-derive.

finding: The two refusals this release adds are specified with opposite evaluation orders and the second one's order is never stated. §4.2.2 pins the mode refusal: "The refusal is evaluated before the mode's own argument validation, so the hint an operator sees names the flag conflict." §4.2.1's name refusal is specified only by its hint — exit 2 "with a hint listing what the invocation would have emitted" — which is a hint that cannot be built without resolving the panel the invocation would produce. §2.2 records that the emitting command "writes repository state as a side effect — it takes the round's snapshot under spec/.tp-review/<base>/", observed twice while this spec was written. So the spec leaves open whether a mistyped --role advances the round snapshot before refusing, and that is not a detail: §6.1 S1 forbids the suite mutating spec/.tp-review/ while §6.2 property 5 requires the exit-2 case be exercised, so the unstated order decides whether those two can both be honoured.
suggestion: State the order in §4.2.1 as §4.2.2 does for its own refusal — the name is validated against the resolved role set before any round-state write, and the hint is built from that resolution. Then §6.2 property 5 is runnable under S1 instead of in tension with it.

finding: §4.2.1 turns a spawned agent that produces nothing into a specified, tested outcome and prices it nowhere. Its own table says `no-checklist-items` drops a prompt but not a unit, so `tp run` still spawns a runner process and a fresh agent context for that role; §4.2.1 then requires the unit's own `tp review <spec> --role <id>` to exit 0 with `prompts: []`, and requires the unit to 'still create its findings file, empty' so `hooks/stop-role-incomplete.sh` lets it stop. §6.2 property 10 makes that path a release requirement ('running it exits 0 — including where the unit set and the emitted set diverge'). The unit's entire product is a zero-byte file. §1.1 accounts for this release to the integer (467 bytes) and §4.3 books the win in bytes (90.6%), while a no-op unit costs a whole agent invocation — a cost orders of magnitude larger than the bytes the same release is optimising — and it appears in neither the cost table nor the Non-Goals. It is not the unit-lifecycle surface §4.4 declines either: `engine.roleUnits` is one filter from applying the same skip, in the same unit derivation §4.2.3 already modifies.
suggestion: Either apply `no-checklist-items` (and, under `--diff-from`, `no-spec-change`) in `roleUnits` so no unit is spawned to write an empty file — at which point §4.2.1's exit-0 branch narrows to the interactive path and property 10's divergence clause has less to carry — or, if that is out of this release's size, price it in §1.1 beside the 467 bytes (one spawned agent per skipped-prompt role per round, producing nothing) and record it in §5 the way Non-Goal 6 records the mirror-image regression defect, with §3.1's honesty about naming no owner.

finding: §6's preamble sets an altitude rule for itself and its first subsection breaks it. The rule: "This section states properties, not tests… The properties below are what an implementation must satisfy; choosing the fixtures, the harness and the assertions is a task's acceptance, which is where tp's own workflow already puts them." §6.1 then rules on the harness in three places: it excludes a specific flag ("--no-state is not one"), it rules out a specific implementation strategy ("relocating the state means relocating the spec"), and it prescribes an assertion ("Those four inputs are pinned by the test"). §6.3 goes further and rules on a Go test idiom ("A TestMain bracket… TestMain is per-package and these tests span packages"), which presumes a package layout no property states. The section that was rewritten to stop prescribing verification is still prescribing it, in the same round it says it stopped — and §7's third paragraph makes the identical claim about itself, so the rule now has two authors and one violation.
suggestion: Restate §6.1 as outcomes and move the ruled-out mechanisms into §6.3, where withdrawn constructions already live and where they read as recorded reasons rather than as constraints. S1's outcome ("running the suite leaves spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ byte-identical") is a property; the three sentences after it are the task's.

finding: Property 11 — "The emitted role set minus the unit set is exactly `{regression}` at a round where `regression` emits, as set equality" — pins only the round, not the command or the mode, and is false in most of the configurations §4.2.2 declares legal. Measured on the shipped binary against an isolated copy of this spec: `--perspective documentation` emits the role `documentation-planner` and nothing else, `--perspective testing` emits `test-planner`, `--verify` emits `verifier`; none of the three is a unit, so emitted-minus-unit is that singleton and not `{regression}`. For `tp audit` the emitted set never contains `regression` at all (`engine.ParseRoleBytes` reserves the id and `roleUnits` derives audit units from the corpus), so under the audit half of properties 4/6/7 the set difference is empty and the property is either false or vacuous depending on which reading an implementer takes. Written as a set equality it reads as a global invariant, which is how a test gets built that fails on a mode the release never intended to constrain — and it is the property §4.4 leans on to make the regression loss "visible", so a false positive here is a repair to the wrong thing.
suggestion: Scope it: "In `tp review`'s default mode at a round where `regression` emits, the emitted role set minus the unit set is exactly `{regression}`." If the audit half is meant to be constrained too, add its own clause — the set difference there is empty and stating that makes the same visibility guarantee for `tp audit` explicit rather than accidental.

finding: §4.2.1's last bullet fixes three behaviours of the flag's own shape — --role takes exactly one value, it is 'not repeatable', and an empty value 'is refused as an unknown role rather than treated as absent, so flag-given-empty and flag-absent are never the same command' — and no property in §6.2 covers any of them. Properties 4, 5 and 6 cover a name that emits, a name that does not, and mode legality. 'Not repeatable' has no stated observable at all: a Go string flag accepts the flag twice with silent last-wins, so an implementation that does exactly that satisfies every property in §6.2 while contradicting §4.2.1's sentence. The empty-value rule is arguably reachable through property 5's exit-2 half only if the reader already decides an empty string is 'a name tp recognises nowhere', which §4.2.1 asserts and §6.2 does not.
suggestion: Add one property covering the flag's shape: the flag given twice, and the flag given an empty value, each produce a stated exit code and hint. If silent last-wins is acceptable for the repeated case, say so in §4.2.1 and delete the 'not repeatable' claim, since as written it is a requirement no test is asked to check.

finding: §4.2.2 states an ordering requirement — the --role refusal 'is evaluated before the mode's own argument validation, so the hint an operator sees names the flag conflict rather than a missing --findings' — and property 6 asserts only the exit code ('refused with exit 2 in every mode that emits none'). Both evaluation orders produce exit 2, so property 6 passes unchanged on an implementation that validates --merge's own arguments first and reports the wrong problem to the operator. The single observable that distinguishes the two orders is the hint's content, and it is fixed nowhere in §6. This matters more than a message usually would, because §4.2.2's ordering is the only thing standing between an operator's typo and a diagnostic about an unrelated missing flag.
suggestion: Extend property 6 with the discriminating observable: in a mode that refuses --role and is simultaneously missing its own required argument, the hint names --role. That single case is the whole content of the ordering claim; without it §4.2.2's sentence is prose no test can refute.

finding: §6.3 is created this round to collect withdrawn constructions, with the right reason — 'listed here rather than beside the properties they used to encumber, so that the properties stay readable and the reasons stay found' — and it is applied to §6 only. Measured on the spec file: 23 of its 123 paragraphs, 11,917 of 40,384 bytes (29.5%), are narrative about drafts that were withdrawn, and only 3 of those lines are in §6.3; the rest sit inline in the normative prose of §1.1, §2.2, §2.3, §2.4, §3.1, §4.1, §4.2.1, §4.2.2, §4.2.3, §4.5 and §7. The cost is not hypothetical, because tp embeds changed sections verbatim into every role prompt under a 6,000-character budget. This round's three modified sections are 7,302 B — §1.1 2,161 B (48% archaeology), §2.3 1,578 B (31%), §4.2.3 3,563 B (66%) — 3,878 B of withdrawn-draft narrative in total. The budget ran out inside §4.2.3 and the changed-sections block truncated ('[...diff content truncated at 6000 chars]', verified in this unit's own prompt), so §6, §6.1, §6.2, §6.3 and §7 — this round's entire new normative surface, about 100 lines — reached every reviewer as ADDED/MODIFIED headings with no text. In a release whose subject is prompt-byte economy, withdrawn drafts displaced the release's actual content from the round's diff.
suggestion: Move each inline obituary into §6.3's table as one row of the shape it already uses (Withdrawn | Why) and cut the narrative from the normative sections; the anti-re-proposal value costs about a line per dead end instead of a paragraph, and it stops being re-emitted every time an unrelated sentence in the same section changes. Removing this round's 3,878 B would have left roughly 2,600 B of the diff budget for §6, the section the round was written to introduce.

finding: §4.1 states as verified fact that the regression prompt's "82,160 bytes reach four units, are assigned to none, and produce no output file." Measured on this spec's round-10 emission, the regression entry carries output_path = .tp/rounds/0.36.0/review-r10/role-regression.ndjson.part — a non-empty path in the round directory. No unit ever writes it, so the outcome §4.1 describes is right, but the payload does assign it a file. The distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic: §2.3 makes non-empty output_path the emission predicate and calls it "a property of the prompt rather than of the role", which silently assumes a named output_path means the prompt has a writer. The regression prompt is a standing counterexample inside the release's own worked measurement, and it is the one §4.4 and Non-Goal 6 already treat as the defect.
suggestion: Change "produce no output file" to "produce no output file, though the payload names one for it" and cite that as the concrete reason §2.3's predicate is over the prompt rather than the role — which is the rationale §2.3 currently attributes to §4.4 and §4.4 does not contain.
